Management reference

Chat Reports Made Simple

A short guide to the chat reports in Fresh: which ones to open first, how to read the team numbers together, what the words mean, and how to turn the numbers into a clear update for the team.

AStart with three questions BReports to open CReading team numbers together DFinding the reports yourself EAll reports at a glance FChanging the dates GJargon buster HTurning numbers into an update
A

Start with three questions

Fresh shows a lot of numbers. Most of them are not needed week to week. These three questions cover what matters for chat, so start here before opening anything else.

1

Are customers being answered quickly?

Long waits are where chat customers leave us.

Look at: SLA compliance rate, then SLA breach contribution (first and next response)

2

Are chats reaching the team and being worked?

Chats that sit, or close without a consultant, are missed opportunities.

Look at: Escalated to human agent, Resolved due to inactivity, Assigned agent

3

Is chat turning into enquiries and bookings?

This is the question that matters most to the business.

Look at: Conversion (fully available once the CRM is live)

More enquiries is not the goal. More bookings is. Enquiry numbers show how busy we are, not how well we are doing. A month with fewer enquiries can still bring in more bookings if more of them convert. When the enquiry count goes up or down, the next question is always: what happened to conversion?
What can wait. Pre-built marketing reports, one-off spikes on a single day, and the wording of bot answers to questions customers have not actually asked. If a number does not help answer one of the three questions above, it can wait.
B

Reports to open

Start at the top and work down. The first reports answer the three questions in Part A. The team activity reports lower down add useful context, and are best read alongside the ones above them.

Click Open in Fresh on any report below to go straight to it, or use the Chat Reports dashboard, which has every report as a one-click tile. The buttons only work for people with access to Analytics in Fresh, and this page holds no customer or team numbers.

Open these first

1

How quickly are we responding?

Answers question 1. Filtered by consultant, it shows their chat count next to how often they met our targets.

Open in Fresh
Our targetsFirst reply: 10 minEvery reply after that: 10 minChat closed within: 30 daysCounted in: business hours
What you see
  • Chats, chats with a target, chats that met it, and the SLA compliance rate
  • SLA breach contribution: which target the missed chats missed
  • The compliance rate day by day
  • Compliance by channel and by group
How to read it

Start with the SLA compliance rate: the share of chats that met our targets. Then look at SLA breach contribution, which shows where the misses happen. A high First Response figure means the misses are mostly slow first replies. A high Next Response figure means conversations stall after the first reply. One chat can miss both, so the two can add up to more than 100%.

Set these filters
  • Date range: a full month
  • Assigned agent name: one consultant at a time, to see their chat count next to how often they met our targets
  • Leave the other filters as they are
Good to know. We have one response target set, and it applies to every chat. The "by SLA policy" chart will always show a single bar, so it can be skipped. Time outside business hours is not counted, so a chat that arrives after hours only starts its 10 minutes when we open.

Report name in Fresh: SLA Compliance Report

2

How is Tommy doing?

In Fresh this report is called Standalone FC - Analyze AI Agent Studio.

Answers question 2: which chats Tommy deals with himself, and which reach the team.

Open in Fresh
Go to the Performance tab

The report opens on Overview. Click Performance in the tabs along the bottom. It shows:

  • The Journey of all Conversations: chats resolved by Tommy, handed to a consultant, or closed because the customer stopped replying
  • WhatsApp against web chat
  • Chats day by day
How to read it

Chats handed to a consultant are the ones the team should be working. Chats closed because the customer stopped replying (Resolved due to Inactivity) are where customers dropped off with Tommy. If that number grows, check Resolved for ready chats that were never handed over.

Set these filters
  • Date range: the last full month, or the last 90 days for the bigger picture
  • Compare against the same length of time before
All nine tabs on this report

The other tabs go into more detail, and most are for checking how Tommy is set up. Overview gives headline totals, but read its deflection rate and thumbs down with care: deflection does not show whether customers were helped, and a thumbs down is a rating on one answer, not a complaint.

3

Is chat turning into enquiries and bookings?

Answers question 3, the one that matters most to the business.

Once the CRM is live
What you will see
  • How many chats became enquiries
  • How many enquiries became bookings
  • Enquiries still open at the end of the day
  • Where enquiries stop moving
Why it is not here yet

Chats need to create enquiries in Fresh before conversion can be counted. Until then, the two reports above and the interim label below are the best guide.

In the meantime
  • Read enquiry numbers next to response times, never on their own
  • Ask what happened to conversion whenever enquiry numbers move
Interim: the Booking Converted label. Until the CRM tracks enquiries through to booking, we are using the Booking Converted chat label to see which chats turned into bookings. It is a stopgap, not the final way of measuring conversion: it only counts chats a consultant labelled, and one customer can have more than one chat. See it per consultant in report 6, and for the team in report 8.

Team activity, read alongside the reports above

4

How many chats came in, and who handled them?

The monthly view of chat volume, when chats arrive, and each consultant's load next to their response times.

Open in Fresh
What you see
  • Average wait, response, interaction and resolution times
  • Chats by WhatsApp and web chat
  • Busiest days, busiest hours, and volume by day of the month
  • Volume handled per consultant
  • Each consultant's first response, response and resolution times
  • Chats by month
How to read it

Read Volume handled per agent and Agent productivity metrics together: how many chats each person handled, next to how quickly they replied. That is the picture Part C explains. Busiest hours and Busiest days show when cover matters most. The row shown as "---" is chats with no consultant recorded.

Set these filters
  • Date range: a full calendar month
  • Compare with the month before, or the same month last year, using the same number of days
  • Check the date on each section: some sections can show a different period to the rest of the page

Report name in Fresh: Monthly Chat Overview Report

5

When are we busiest?

The days and hours when chats come in, so chat cover can match demand.

Open in Fresh
What you see
  • Busiest Days: chats by day of the week
  • Busiest Hours: chats by hour of the day
  • Chat volume by Day of Month: patterns across the month
  • Chats by month
How to read it

Look for the hours and days that stand out, then compare them with who was online at those times (report 7). Peaks with thin cover are where wait times grow and chats are missed. Patterns across the month help plan ahead.

Set these filters
  • Date range: a full month, or three months for a steadier picture
  • These sections sit in the Monthly Chat Overview Report: scroll down to find them

Report name in Fresh: Monthly Chat Overview Report (Busiest Days and Busiest Hours sections)

6

How is each consultant closing their chats?

The label each consultant chose when closing a chat, shown per person.

Open in Fresh
What you see
  • Chats per consultant, split by label
  • Labels such as Booking Converted, Assistance with a booking, Information only and Phoning client
  • Chats with no label, shown as "---"

Tip: hover over any bar to see that label broken down by consultant, for example how many Booking Converted chats each person closed.

How to read it

Look at the mix for each person, not just the total. Booking Converted is how we track chats that turned into bookings for now (interim). A high share of Information only on chats that looked like real enquiries is worth a look together. Many chats show "---" because Tommy closes inactive chats without a label.

Set these filters
  • Date range: last month
  • Channel, status and assigned agent can narrow it down
  • Labels only count when a consultant chooses one, so the picture is as good as the labelling

Report name in Fresh: New Label Report

7

When were consultants online?

How long each consultant was set as available for chats, down to every session.

Open in Fresh
What you see
  • Each consultant's average time online per day
  • A team average in the Grand Total row
  • Underneath: every session, with start time, end time and duration
How to read it

Being online shows someone was available, not what they did with the time. It is most useful for spotting gaps in cover across the day. It is an average, so one very long session lifts it a lot: check the sessions before reading anything into a high number.

Read it with

Chats handled and response times (report 4), busiest times (report 5) and targets met (report 1). Part C shows how they fit together.

Digging into the detail

The first view is only a summary. The useful detail sits underneath it.

  1. Open the report. The first table shows each consultant's Average availability duration.
  2. Hover over the table and click the Expand icon (two small arrows) at its top right. The underlying data is only available in the expanded view.
  3. In the expanded view, scroll down and click Show underlying data to see every session: Start time, End time and Duration in seconds.
  4. To see one consultant's breakdown in the table, click the arrow next to their name.
Reading seconds. 3,600 seconds is 1 hour, and 5,400 seconds is 1.5 hours, the length of one daily chat shift.
Very long sessions. A session that runs overnight usually means someone did not set themselves offline at the end of their shift. In the example, Agent G shows an average of almost 19 hours because one session ran from Thursday afternoon to Friday morning. It inflates the average, so it is a reminder to give, not a sign of extra work.

Report name in Fresh: Agent Availability Report

Day-to-day check

8

Is anything sitting today?

A quick daily look to keep chats moving, plus customer ratings and how chats were closed.

Open in Fresh
What you see
  • Chats started and resolved, with trends
  • Average wait, first response, response and resolution times
  • Chats by status: resolved, assigned, waiting on customer, waiting on internal team
  • Customer ratings (CSAT) and the average score
  • Chats by channel and by label
How to read it

Start with Conversations volume by status. Chats still assigned or waiting on the internal team are the ones to pick up today. Conversation volume by label category shows how chats were closed, including Booking Converted, which we use for now to track chats that turned into bookings (interim). It only counts chats a consultant labelled. One day's numbers move for many reasons, so leave judging performance to the monthly reports.

Set these filters
  • It opens on the last 30 days
  • For the daily check, change the dates to today, or to yesterday first thing in the morning

Report name in Fresh: Daily Monitor

Need more than these show? These reports are built for the team to use day to day without waiting on anyone. For a deeper comparison or a question they cannot answer, I can help.
C

Reading team numbers together

Time online, chats handled and response times each tell part of the story. Read together, they show whether a shift is working and where support is needed. Read alone, any one of them can point in the wrong direction.

Three numbers, one picture

  • Time online shows availability.
  • Chats handled shows load.
  • Response times show how well that load was handled.

Common patterns and what they usually mean

Working well

Plenty of chats, good first and next response

The shift is running as it should. Worth recognising.

Stretched

Plenty of chats, weak next response

Chats are being picked up but the consultant cannot keep up. Look at the load on that shift before looking at the person.

Quiet shift

Online for the shift, few chats

Often a quiet time of day, or chats going to someone else. Check how chats were shared before drawing a conclusion.

Worth a conversation

Few chats, slow responses

A good moment for a supportive one-to-one, looking at a few of their real chats together.

Compare like with like. Every consultant does a daily chat shift, so compare people over the same full month rather than single days.
One number is never the full story. Before raising a number with a consultant, check the other two and look at a few of their actual chats. Spot Checking Chats shows how to find and open them.
D

Finding the reports yourself

The Open in Fresh buttons in Part B are the quickest way in. If you need to find a report another way, Fresh splits its reports into three areas: Sales, Marketing and Support. The chat reports are under Support Analytics.

  1. Open Fresh at cullinanholdings-org.freshworks.com.
  2. In the menu down the left, select the Analytics icon (the small bar chart).
  3. Choose Support Analytics.
  4. Open the report by its name:
    • SLA Compliance Report
    • Standalone FC - Analyze AI Agent Studio
    • Monthly Chat Overview Report
    • New Label Report
    • Agent Availability Report
    • Daily Monitor

Email or Fresh: which to use

Some reports also arrive by email on a schedule. The email is a handy reminder, but it is a snapshot: the numbers for a fixed period, as they were when it was sent. The same report opened in Fresh holds much richer information, because the detail behind every number is there to work with.

The email is good for

  • A quick glance at the headline numbers
  • A reminder that it is time to look
  • Keeping a record of a period

Open it in Fresh to

  • Change the dates, and compare periods of the same length
  • Filter by consultant, channel or group
  • Hover over the small "i" to see exactly what a number means
  • Hover over a bar on a chart to see the breakdown behind it, for example by consultant
  • Export the detail to a spreadsheet. Large exports can be slow to download, so having the export emailed is usually quicker
  • See today's position, not the position when the email was sent
Best read in Fresh. The SLA Compliance Report, the Monthly Chat Overview Report and the Daily Monitor are all much more useful opened in Fresh. Use the email as the nudge, then click through to the report.

I manage the email schedule, so let me know if a report should be added, changed or stopped.

F

Changing the dates

Every report has a date setting near the top. Changing it is the most useful thing to know.

  1. Open the report and find the date setting near the top of the page. It often shows a preset such as Last quarter.
  2. Click it and choose Custom.
  3. Pick a start date and an end date, then apply.
  4. Check the dates shown on the report match what you picked before you read any numbers.

Choose a month, not a week

Week-to-week numbers move for reasons that have nothing to do with how the team is working, so they tend to cause worry rather than give answers. Look at full months, or the last four weeks against the four before.

  • Travel enquiries follow their own rhythm. Paydays, school holidays, public holidays, specials and weather all push one week up and the next down.
  • A week is a small sample. A few busy days can make a normal week look like a problem, or a slow week look fine.
  • Bookings take longer than a week. Many customers chat, get a quote and book weeks later, so a weekly view shows the enquiry but not the result.
  • The latest week is never finished. Chats and quotes are still open, so it will always look weaker than it really is.
Compare like with like. When comparing two periods, use the same number of days for both, for example 1 to 30 September against 1 to 30 October. Different lengths give misleading totals.
Check the presets. Presets like "Last quarter" do not always cover the months you expect. Custom dates remove the guesswork. The current month will also show more open chats, because some are still in progress.
G

Jargon buster

Plain-English meanings for the words on the chat reports. For Fresh's own wording, hover over the small "i" next to any number on a report.

Chats initiatedVolume
Every chat that was started, including ones where the customer said nothing further.
ChannelVolume
Where the chat came in: web chat (the pop-up on the website) or WhatsApp.
Web chatVolume
The Live Chat pop-up on the website.
TopicSetup
The option a customer picks when they open chat, for example "Chat to us". It decides who answers first.
Wait timeSpeed
How long a customer waits from when the chat is handed to the team until a consultant first replies. Time with the bot is not included.
Response timeSpeed
The average gap between a customer's message and the consultant's reply, across the whole chat. It includes time spent pricing or checking things mid-chat.
Business hoursSpeed
Wait and response times only count the hours we are open. Time after hours is not counted.
Interaction timeSpeed
How long the chat was open overall, from start to close.
Resolution timeSpeed
How long it took for the chat to be marked resolved. Long times often mean chats were left open rather than closed.
ResolvedOutcome
The chat has been closed. It does not tell you whether the customer was helped or booked.
Resolved by botOutcome
Tommy closed the chat without a consultant, either because he answered the question or the customer stopped replying.
Auto-resolvedOutcome
Tommy closes a chat automatically after about a day with no reply from the customer. These chats have no label.
Resolved by consultantOutcome
A consultant closed the chat.
Not resolvedOutcome
Chats still open. A high number can mean chats are sitting and need picking up.
HandoverBot
When Tommy passes a chat to the team. Some chats that are ready do not get handed over and need checking in Resolved.
Bot drop-offBot
When a customer stops replying to Tommy. Report 2 shows how many, as Resolved due to inactivity. Spot check a few of those chats to see where they stopped.
Assigned agentPeople
The consultant the chat was given to.
GroupPeople
The team a chat is sent to before a consultant picks it up.
Agent availabilityPeople
Whether a consultant was set as online and able to take chats.
LabelOutcome
The reason a consultant chooses when closing a chat, for example a new enquiry or an information request.
StatusOutcome
Where a chat is right now, for example assigned, waiting on customer, waiting on internal team, or resolved.
SLASpeed
Service level: the response times we aim to meet. Ours are 10 minutes for the first reply, 10 minutes for every reply after that, and 30 days to close a chat, counted in business hours.
SLA breachSpeed
A chat that missed one of our targets.
SLA compliance rateSpeed
Chats that met our targets, as a share of all chats that have a target.
SLA breach contributionSpeed
Of the chats that missed a target, the share that missed the first reply target and the share that missed a later one. One chat can miss both, so the two can add up to more than 100%.
First responseSpeed
The first reply once a chat reaches the team. Target: within 10 minutes.
Next responseSpeed
Every reply after the first one. Fresh settings call this "every response time". Target: within 10 minutes. Shows whether a conversation keeps moving.
SLA policySetup
The set of response targets a chat is measured against. We have one default policy that applies to all chats.
Deflection rateBot
Fresh's measure of chats Tommy dealt with without a consultant. Hover over the small "i" on the report to see exactly how it is counted, and check the journey of conversations to see how many Tommy actually answered.
Escalated to human agentBot
Chats Tommy handed to a consultant.
Resolved due to inactivityBot
Chats closed because the customer stopped replying.
Topic distributionBot
The subjects customers chat about, for example travel planning and bookings, sorted by Fresh.
Knowledge sourceBot
The website pages, FAQs and documents Tommy uses to answer questions.
Positive and negative feedbackBot
Thumbs up or thumbs down from customers on a single answer from Tommy. A thumbs down is not a complaint.
CSATOutcome
Customer satisfaction: the rating a customer gives at the end of a chat, from 1 to 5. Only some customers leave one.
Waiting on customerOutcome
A chat status: we have replied and are waiting for the customer.
Waiting on internal teamOutcome
A chat status: the customer is waiting on us. These are the ones to pick up.
Re-openedOutcome
A resolved chat that the customer started again.
Busiest hoursVolume
The hours of the day when most chats start. Useful for planning chat cover.
WorkflowBot
A set path Tommy follows, for example the introduction or handing a chat to the team.
ConversionSales
A chat that became an enquiry or a booking. Fully tracked once the CRM goes live.
Daily averageMethod
A total divided by the number of days. Use it to compare periods of different lengths fairly.
Interaction IDMethod
Fresh's reference number for a chat. On reports it cannot be clicked to open the chat.
ExportMethod
Downloads the report as a spreadsheet so the numbers can be checked or combined outside Fresh.

No match. Try a shorter word.

H

Turning numbers into an update

A good update gives the team one clear message. It names what changed, what it means, and what happens next. Three short lines are enough.

1. What changed

One number, compared to something. "Up" or "down" only means something next to the period before.

2. What it means

Why it matters for customers or bookings, in one sentence.

3. What we are doing

The one action, who owns it, and when we will look again.

Example shape, fill in your own numbers

What changed: Average wait time this month was [X minutes], compared to [Y minutes] last month.

What it means: Customers who wait longer may leave before a consultant replies, which can cost us enquiries.

What we are doing: During chat shifts, pick up new chats before finishing quotes. We will check the number again on [date].

Before sharing a number, check

  • Do the dates on the report match the period I am talking about?
  • Am I comparing periods of the same length, or using daily averages?
  • Is this one day or one week, or a pattern over a month or more?
  • If I am sharing an enquiry number, have I said what happened to conversion too?
  • If it is about a person, have I read it with their chat count and the other team numbers in Part C?
  • Does it answer one of the three questions in Part A?
